transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Ethan Rivera (CTO - Pegasus), Priya Nair (Head ML - Pegasus), Jon Park (Platform Eng - Pegasus)

Summary:
Quick parity/migration demo and workshop focused on the runtime adapter strategy: how Pegasus moves endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API, expected delta on latency and cost, migration risks (KV cache, batching, tokenization), and a short plan for a 1-week pilot to validate production metrics. Agreed to share cost spreadsheet, bench logs and schedule pilot kickoff.

Topics covered:
- Migration approach: adapter vs rewrite
- Runtime differences: kv cache, continuous batching, kernel/quantization impacts
- Security & compliance: SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, data residency
- Cost/latency tradeoffs: hosted vs dedicated vs private
- Console walkthrough: rollouts, per-route tracing, quality eval hooks

Action items (captured again in metadata): see action_items field

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this pretty pragmatic. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side. We have Liam, our SE, on the call too. Ethan, Priya, Jon, you good to go?
[00:12] Ethan: Yep, all set. Thanks Maya.
[00:15] Priya: Hi, thanks. We sent over a short deck, hope that's okay.
[00:18] Maya: Yep saw the deck, thank you. Quick agenda: parity map, demo of the API + console, then an ops/cost sprint and next steps. We have... we only have 50 minutes so we'll move quick.
[00:30] Liam: I'll start with the adapter approach and show a tiny demo app hitting Redwood's API with an OpenAI-compatible shim. It's a simple change - mostly header+model-name mapping and tokenization nuances.
[00:41] Jon: For context, our main constraint is multi-tenant throughput - we run roughly 9k requests per minute at peak, median prompt length 220 tokens, and we care a lot about p95 latency. Also strict egress rules from our VPC.
[00:55] Maya: Great detail, thanks. That P95 goal will guide whether we recommend hosted for rapid onramp or Dedicated for predictable throughput.
[01:05] Priya: Also, we use Anthropic for assistant flows and Together for some specialized instruction tuning. We need feature parity on streaming and function-calling.
[01:20] Liam: Streaming and function-calling are available on Redwood hosted — same API shapes are supported; we also do chunked streaming and tool calling. One caveat: for Together models the prompt formatting sometimes needs small changes because of tokenization differences, we can show the tokenizer diff.
[01:35] Priya: Great. How about kv cache behavior? We rely on prefix caching heavily for convo state.
[01:44] Liam: Redwood's runtime exposes KV cache semantics compatible with typical LLM runtimes; there was a minor voice of mismatch early on — sometimes you see different cache keying when the model's tokenizer merges tokens differently. We account for that in the adapter with a small normalization layer.
[01:58] Ethan: When you say adapter, is that code we run in our infra or you provide a managed compatibility shim?
[02:06] Maya: Both options. For quick proofs we provide an OpenAI-compatible shim (hosted) you can point to and it rewrites requests. For production we usually recommend either (a) a simple in-house adapter that tweaks headers + tokenization, or (b) use Redwood Dedicated/Private with a config mapping — that avoids proxy latency.
[02:26] Jon: Latency matters. The shim adds what, 20-40ms?
[02:31] Liam: For the hosted shim, under normal conditions it's low tens of milliseconds; worst case we've observed up to ~120ms under noisy neighbors but we have autoscaling and fallbacks. If you need strict p95 bounds, Dedicated gives you a much tighter SLA.
[02:45] Priya: Can we see the console? We want to understand rollout and regression monitoring.
[02:49] Maya: Sure, Liam will share the console. (screen share noise)
[02:56] Liam: Alright, opening Redwood Console. Route view -> here you can see per-route token cost, latency heatmaps, and per-model traces. We also have the eval hooks — you can upload a prompt set and we auto-run quality checks on each model update.
[03:15] Priya: Nice, is eval tied to alerts?
[03:18] Liam: Yes - quality regressions can create alerts and block rollouts. You can set thresholds for BLEU-ish metrics or custom classifier checks.
[03:25] Ethan: About cost, we need a clear matrix: current spend on Anthropic/OpenAI vs expected on Redwood, including tokenization differences and batch sizing.
[03:34] Maya: We'll send a tailored cost model. Quick note: tokenization variance can swing token counts by ~2-6% depending on model; batching and kv cache tend to be the larger drivers of unit cost.
[03:46] Jon: Any guidance for batching? Our 220-token median - do you auto-batch?
[03:52] Liam: Redwood uses continuous batching with heuristics driven by latency SLOs. You can tune batch windows; we propose starting with a small 20ms window and ramp to 40ms for higher throughput. That gives you 2-3x throughput improvement typically while p95 remains within acceptable bounds.
[04:08] Priya: When you say quantization recommendations, how invasive is that for model behavior? Our QA team is sensitive to hallucination regressions.
[04:18] Maya: Optimize recommends quant profile by workload — e.g., 4-bit PTQ for high-throughput generation tasks where slight differences are tolerable, mixed int8 for instruction-tuned models where fidelity is critical. We always strongly recommend gating quantized models behind evals so you can detect regressions quickly.
[04:38] Ethan: Security — we have to hit SOC 2 + internal pen test before we can onboard anything third-party. What are your options?
[04:46] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and can share the attestation. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering or on-prem. We also provide audit logs and per-token traceability in the console.
[04:59] Jon: Egress - can we restrict outbound to certain IPs?
[05:04] Liam: For Redwood Hosted we provide static egress ranges and support VPC peering in certain regions; Dedicated and Private eliminate egress concerns because you run inside your network or our reserved pool inside your VPC.
[05:17] Priya: Cool. Could you give a quick walkthrough of migrating an endpoint from OpenAI-style code to Redwood — like what are the code diffs?
[05:26] Liam: Sure - I'll share a minimal node example. (typing) Old: openai.createChatCompletion with model name and messages. New: a single POST to /v1/generate with body {model: "redwood-rt-large", input: ..., stream: true} if you want streaming. We also support function calling via the same patterns. The main diffs: adjust header names (Authorization stays bearer), map parameter names, and handle tokenization idiosyncrasies.
[05:56] Priya: Any gotchas with function-calling? We rely heavily on structured outputs.
[06:00] Liam: We support JSON schema enforcement + function call capture; the console surface shows mismatches in the evals. One common gotcha: Together models sometimes return alternatives or variations in the function call name casing; adapter normalizes casing.
[06:15] Ethan: Performance question: what hardware profiles do you use for Dedicated? We want GPU-level details because some of our models are heavy.
[06:22] Liam: Dedicated runs on A100 class for large mdoels or A10/A30 for smaller ones depending on your committed capacity; runtime will pin optimized kernels and choose quantized paths where possible. For private on-prem we support customer hardware but you get more ops overhead.
[06:38] Maya: Quick note: we have a bench script we'll share that runs sample prompts at scale across a few model variants so you can see token/sec, p95, and memory footprints.
[06:49] Priya: Good. Question on data retention: can we auto-delete request/response pairs after X days? We need 30-day retention only.
[06:58] Liam: Yes policy-based retention windows are configurable at route-level; logs can be exported to customer S3 too.
[07:06] Jon: Okay can we talk about canary and rollback how it works?
[07:09] Liam: Canary is router-level: you set a percentage or user subset, we collect traces and quality evals. If you hit regression thresholds the rollout pauses and optionally falls back to the previous model. You can also set automatic fallback to a cheaper model if capacity spikes.
[07:27] Ethan: That fallback sounds valuable. How do you define compatibility between models during fallback? For example, Together -> Redwood equivalency.
[07:36] Maya: We map model families and recommend candidates that preserve instruction tuning characteristics. We'll provide a parity mapping table — e.g., Together-instruct-xx -> redwood-instruct-yy, plus notes about tokenizer impact and recommended temp/top_p adjustments.
[07:51] Priya: Could you show the parity table real quick?
[07:54] Liam: (shares link) Here's an initial parity sheet: https://redwood.example.com/parity/pegasus-parity-v1 - this is a sample link, we'll send the real doc. It includes model mapping, expected token delta, and recommended batch and quant profiles.
[08:10] Jon: I see notes about "kvk cache" in the doc, what does that mean?
[08:13] Liam: Sorry bad note — meant KV cache. Transcription/typo on that sheet, we'll clean it up.
[08:20] Priya: On the pilot: what does a 1-week pilot look like operationally?
[08:24] Maya: Typically first 2 days are integration and run a baseline; next 3 days we run traffic shaping and parity bench; final 2 days we collect evals and confirm rollouts or tweaks. We'll provide the bench harness and a sample dataset.
[08:38] Ethan: Are there any licensing or model provenance issues? Some of our regulatory reviewers ask about model lineage.
[08:45] Liam: We label model provenance in the console and maintain a model catalog with versioned artifacts and licensing metadata. For open models we include the license; for any redwood-curated models we include notes.
[08:56] Priya: Let's talk about tokenization differences - can you quantify worst-case?
[09:01] Liam: Worst-case we've seen ~10% token delta on very markup-heavy inputs; typical is 2-5%. We recommend calibrating cost projections with a sample of your production prompts.
[09:15] Maya: Quick poll - would Pegasus prefer Hosted shim for faster time-to-value or Dedicated for stricter SLA?
[09:22] Ethan: For the first wave we'd take Hosted for speed but likely move to Dedicated once we validate parity.
[09:29] Priya: Agreed, Hosted then Dedicated. But we need a clear roll plan.
[09:33] Maya: Great. Liam, can you run a short demo bench now?
[09:37] Liam: Yep - I'll run a small script (it's not full scale but shows the pattern). Running against a 1000-sample prompt set — measuring p50/p95 and token/sec.
[09:45] (keyboard clacks)
[10:02] Liam: Alright results: redwood-hosted with default batching: p50 ~ 110ms, p95 ~ 420ms for this sample on an instruction-style model; token/sec ~ 1200. When I toggle batch window to 30ms p95 drops to ~320ms and token/sec increases to ~1500.
[10:22] Priya: That's promising. How noisy is that under multi-tenant?
[10:26] Liam: This run is isolated; in multi-tenant we've seen occasional spikes — that's why we recommend starting with dedicated or a burst capacity plan if you have strict SLAs.
[10:36] Jon: For Dedicated, what's the typical onboarding time?
[10:39] Maya: Provisioning Dedicated usually 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region. Private on-prem longer.
[10:46] Ethan: Are there penalties for moving from Hosted to Dedicated? Any data migration headaches?
[10:51] Liam: No penalties; migration is mostly config and routing changes. Data can be kept in your logs or exported and then attached to the Dedicated account.
[10:59] Priya: Can you integrate with our existing observability stack? We use Datadog and Sentry.
[11:04] Liam: We have hooks and exporters for Datadog/OpenTelemetry. Sentry-style error capture can be forwarded via webhooks.
[11:11] Ethan: Ok, security follow-ups: can you share SOC 2 report and the network diagram for Hosted egress ranges?
[11:16] Maya: Yes, I'll attach SOC 2 and the egress range doc in the follow-up email.
[11:21] Maya: Quick aside - a few gotchas we've seen during ports: tokenization differences causing prompt truncation, function-calling schema mismatches, and caching mis-keying. We typically provide a short test harness to catch these early.
[11:36] Priya: About telemetry: will you preserve request ids so we can stitch traces end-to-end?
[11:41] Liam: Yes we surface request_id and allow custom request_id passthrough so you can correlate app logs with model traces.
[11:47] Jon: Anything special for fine-tuned models? We tune a few internally.
[11:51] Liam: Fine-tuned models are supported — you can bring-your-own model artifact on Private or we can host fine-tuned checkpoints under a private namespace. For hosted, we may curb large custom model hosting depending on size/cost but it's doable.
[12:06] Ethan: About the bench - can we run the bench with our dev team and you observe?
[12:11] Maya: Absolutely, that's part of the pilot. We'll pair on the first run.
[12:15] Priya: Cost detail - do you account for tokenization differences in the billing or we just get billed raw tokens?
[12:21] Liam: Billing is based on tokens counted by the runtime. We provide tools to project token deltas and plug into the cost model. We'll show a sample spreadsheet.
[12:30] (short pause)
[12:40] Ethan: Anything on SSO? We need SAML 2.0 and SCIM provisioning.
[12:45] Maya: Yes we support SAML 2.0 and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll share the SSO quickstart doc.
[12:52] Priya: For the adapter code, do you have a JS/Go example?
[12:56] Liam: Yes both. I'll drop a github gist after the call. It's a 20-line shim for simple cases.
[13:03] Priya: Could you show an example where tokenization changed a conversation?
[13:07] Liam: (pulls an example) Here's a Together prompt with heavy markdown; token delta was 9% and in one case caused a missing stop token which truncated assistant output. The adapter inserts explicit stop sequences and normalizes token boundaries.
[13:25] Ethan: That could be problematic for structured outputs; good to know.
[13:29] Maya: We'll include that case in the bench suite.
[13:33] Priya: Ok, another question: do you support region pinning for data residency?
[13:37] Liam: Yes — route-level region pinning and region-aware routing policies.
[13:42] Ethan: If we run the pilot and like results, what's the commercial path? Trial credits -> committed Dedicated -> enterprise support?
[13:50] Maya: Typical path: self-serve pilot or sales-assisted trial -> commit to Dedicated or Private for SLA -> enterprise contract and support. We can put a pilot SOW together if needed.
[14:00] Jon: About deployment knobs in Optimize - any recommended defaults for an instruction-tuned assistant?
[14:05] Liam: Default: batch window 20-30ms, kv cache enabled, top_p 0.9 and temperature 0.2 for assistant flows. Quantization: avoid 4-bit on the main assistant until you validate with evals.
[14:18] Priya: Could you repeat details for function-calling mismatch handling?
[14:22] Liam: Adapter normalizes names, enforces schema at the runtime and we capture mismatches as part of evals; console surfaces those as failing cases.
[14:31] Maya: Quick sanity check, folks - any red flags so far about switching?
[14:35] Ethan: No red flags; mostly operational questions and verifying performance.
[14:39] Priya: Same. We need to confirm internal security review timeline.
[14:42] Maya: Great - we'll follow up with docs and the cost sheet.
[14:46] (short pause)
[15:00] Liam: I'm going to share the bench logs now and a short runbook link: https://redwood.example.com/runbooks/pegasus-onramp-2026-11
[15:10] (link posted)
[15:16] Priya: I see a note about "fallback to smaller model" in the runbook - is that automatic?
[15:20] Liam: It's configurable. If you hit capacity thresholds the router can auto-route a percentage of traffic to a pre-configured fallback model. That's useful for graceful degradation.
[15:33] Jon: For SLA we'd want a playbook on rate limiting and how clients should handle 429s.
[15:39] Maya: We'll include an SDK sample for exponential backoff and recommended retry windows.
[15:45] Ethan: Regarding compliance — can logs be redacted for PII automatically?
[15:50] Liam: Yes we have redaction pipelines and tokens can be masked or removed before storing. That can be set per-route.
[15:58] Priya: Ok next - let's confirm the timeline: we want a pilot the week of 11/22 and a security review the week of 11/15. Can you meet those?
[16:07] Maya: Yes, we'll aim to deliver materials by 11/12 to start the security review on 11/15 and pilot 11/22.
[16:15] Ethan: Sounds good.
[16:18] Jon: Any estimated cost delta percent range you can share now?
[16:22] Maya: Ballpark depends on model family and quantization but I'd say expected cost parity +/- 10-20% for hosted with default configs; you can often reduce unit cost by 30-50% via batching and caching in steady state. We'll give exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[16:38] Priya: Great. If we identify regressions during the pilot, what's the escalation path?
[16:44] Liam: SE triage -> rollback policy -> if needed, direct on-call escalation to infra team. We'll include contact details in the SOW.
[16:52] Ethan: One last question - do you support per-customer model namespaces so we don't conflict with other tenants?
[16:57] Liam: Yes, for Dedicated and Private you get isolated namespaces. Hosted can also provide private namespaces for enterprise customers.
[17:06] Maya: Alright let's recap next steps.
[17:08] Maya: We'll send: SOC 2, egress ranges, parity mapping sheet, bench harness + runbook link, cost spreadsheet and a small adapter gist.
[17:16] Ethan: We'll share: sample prompt set, success criteria, and internal security contacts.
[17:21] Priya: We'll also provide a short list of high-risk flows that need extra testing.
[17:26] Maya: Great. Action items recorded; we'll follow up via email and attach docs. Thanks everyone for the time.
[17:34] Ethan: Thanks, very helpful.
[17:36] Priya: Thank you.
[17:38] Jon: Thanks all.
[17:40] Maya: Bye.

(Transcript ends - note: timestamps in body are approximate sampling markers; full audio had normal conversational overlap, occasional microphone lag. A couple of proper nouns may be mis-transcribed - we cleaned obvious typos where possible.)
